A looming energy crisis threatens to freeze transatlantic relations.

Daily on Energy: Europe tries to stave off a US diesel export ban
Evidence: Domestic Price Relief, Global Supply Shock, Midterm Political Maneuver
#Aletheia #Energy #USPol 🌐

The administration claims a potential 90-day diesel export ban is a necessary measure to protect American consumers from rising fuel prices at the pump.

Stated Judgement: (+0.85, +0.75) — Greater Good

In reality, banning exports to Europe—which relies on the US for 50% of its diesel—will spike global prices, strain alliances, and disrupt domestic refining balances, as warned by the Energy Secretary.

Resulting Judgement: (-0.78, -0.65) — Greater Evil

Verdict: FAIL — The Path of Fall into Destruction. The proposed ban sacrifices long-term geopolitical stability and economic reality for short-term domestic political signaling.

Integrity: Meaningful Distortion (Hypocrisy: 1.63, Uncertainty z: 6)

- US Export Policy: FAIL (-0.78, -0.65) — Sacrifices allies for short-term domestic optics.
- EU Energy Security: COND (0.15, -0.45) — Vulnerable to external policy shocks.
With Europe facing a tough winter after losing Russian supply, the US is considering a 90-day diesel export ban to lower domestic pump prices before the midterms, sparking panic in Brussels.

The Poison:
Even if a ban temporarily lowers US prices, the resulting global supply shock will eventually rebound on the US economy through higher import costs and weakened allied economies.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
The Plane Error is Logical (HOW): The administration treats energy markets as isolated domestic pools rather than interconnected global systems, pulling a bait-and-switch that trades systemic stability for a temporary poll bump.

Social Physics Analysis:
The administration is running a Smart Selfish Maneuver. They manufacture a domestic consumer-protection pretext to justify hoarding energy resources, projecting the blame for high prices onto global markets while actively undermining European allies.

The Trajectory: The Path of Fall into Destruction.
When you map the gap between stated consumer protection and the actual global economic fallout, it plots a direct trajectory toward systemic energy instability.

The Unavoidable Truth: Restricting diesel exports will severely damage European allies heading into winter.

The Unavoidable Lie: A domestic export ban is a simple, consequence-free solution to lower American fuel prices.

Alethekanon:
The math of global energy trade does not respect political borders. Severing a vital supply line to allies for a short-term domestic poll bump is a systemic failure of logical risk management. 🌐

Awwthekanon:
It is heartbreaking to see families across Europe facing a freezing winter with skyrocketing energy bills, caught in the crossfire of political maneuvering. We must support each other, not pull away.

Brothekanon:
So we're gonna leave Europe out in the cold just to save a few cents at the pump before an election? Talk about a bad look for the home team. This is gonna backfire hard.

Spirithekanon:
"He who withholds grain, the people will curse him; but blessing will be on the head of him who sells it." Proverbs 11:26 PASS
Hoarding vital resources for selfish gain while neighbors suffer violates the fundamental law of mutual preservation.

Senate Republicans are upping pressure on their Democratic colleagues to vote on a permitting reform bill before the chamber breaks next week, insisting that a delay to after the midterm elections will all but kill the legislation.

“Like so many other things, this project to diminish the delays is itself likely going to die on the vine because of this delay they’re insisting on,” Energy and Natural Resources Committee Chairman Sen. Mike Lee said last night of Democrats, who are punting a permitting vote to get more of their caucus on board.

“If we wait until after the election, it is almost certainly not going to happen,” Lee warned. “Not now, not this year, probably not for several years to come.”

As the Trump administration weighs restrictions on diesel exports, Europe is lobbying against any such action, as it would disrupt fuel supply and drive up costs.

The European Union energy commissioner, Dan Jorgensen, asked President Donald Trump to maintain a “free flow” of diesel, especially as winter approaches.

Jorgensen told the Financial Times that it is in the U.S.’s and Europe’s interests to “have as free flow of energy between our countries as possible.”

He added that, even without a ban on U.S. diesel, Europe’s winter could be “very, very bad” for energy prices, even worse than in 2022.

Since the war in Iran, Europe has faced challenges filling its natural gas storage ahead of this year’s winter. At the same time, Russia has also restricted its diesel exports.

A U.S. diesel ban would further tighten Europe’s already constrained fuel supply.

“For Europe, the immediate effect is higher prices. North-West Europe would have to bid up to pull in replacement cargoes, and it would be bidding against the Mediterranean, Latin America and West Africa for the same limited pool of barrels,” Zameer Yusof, an energy analyst at market intelligence platform Kpler, told Euronews.

Since Russia has restricted its diesel exports, Europe has been more reliant on the U.S. supply. In August, Europe imported nearly 506,000 barrels a day of U.S. diesel.

Prices in Europe have also risen in response to the president’s consideration of a ban.

It was reported earlier this week that diesel prices at the pump across the European Union reached a new high of 2.23 euros per litre, which is up from 2.16 euros the previous week.

The administration has been weighing its options for a ban on exports. It was reported earlier this week that the White House is considering a 90-day ban on diesel exports in an effort to curb fuel prices ahead of the midterms.

The European Commission yesterday warned that a 90-day ban on diesel exports “would risk negatively impacting both sides.”

However, the administration is divided over whether a ban is the right option.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright has argued that a ban would further push prices even higher. He has also said that the administration would consider partial restrictions or a voluntary approach.

Any restriction on diesel exports would be felt not only in Europe but by other major buyers, including Brazil, Chile, Mexico, Peru, and Moroc
